title: The Fed Is Worried AI Agents Could Trigger a Bank Run
excerpt: The Fed warns AI agents could trigger rapid bank runs, while billions in AI infrastructure debt are finding their way into life insurance.
content_html:
If you’re worried that the artificial intelligence bubble might pop, tanking the stock market and quickly plummeting the value of your personal investment and retirement accounts, maybe you’ll find some solace in the fact that there are apparently some way more absurd ways that artificial intelligence could upend our financial institutions and plunge us all into an instant recession.

Take this scenario that is apparently high enough on the Federal Reserve’s radar that one of their governors decided to bring it up at the Computing Machinery International Conference in Milan, Italy, on Monday: swarms of AI agents creating bank runs.

“Where customers once needed to execute transfers, AI agents could instantaneously detect yield differentials or stability signals and autonomously move funds at high speed, potentially accelerating runs that unfold in minutes, overwhelming traditional liquidity management and regulatory intervention timelines,” Barr said as part of his prepared remarks, according to Bloomberg.

Now, maybe that is the result of a bunch of AI agents with specific orders acting autonomously at the same time, creating unexpected and unmanageable volume. Or, maybe, Barr warned, banks could face agents attempting to do things they aren’t authorized to do. Banks would then have to discern whether those requests were legitimate, and could be overwhelmed. Axios reported earlier this year that banks are already identifying agents attempting to access customer accounts without the banks’ authorization, sometimes apparently acting beyond their users’ instructions. So it’s far from inconceivable.

Barr also warned of some less technical concerns, as well, per Bloomberg, including more than $3 trillion in potential off-balance-sheet obligations related to AI infrastructure spending and circular financing deals between the major players in the space who are seemingly just passing the same money around.

Funny he should mention that, because the New York Times recently highlighted how these companies aren’t just putting their venture capital funders’ and giant investment banks’ money on the line—they’ve also roped in the insurance companies backing millions of Americans’ life insurance policies.

Per the report, some creative bookkeeping has resulted in the insurance industry becoming increasingly tied up in AI spending, with American life insurers like Athene and Corebridge Financial holding $85.2 billion in AI-related debt as of June, according to Moody’s. Barclays separately estimates that life insurers own about 15% of all AI data center debt. Moody’s projects that insurers’ AI investments could climb as high as $185 billion by the end of 2027.

And they do it all by obscuring the investments: The Times pointed to an arrangement that xAI made that involved creating a financial entity that would borrow the money to buy chips that xAI needed and lease those chips to the company. Because that firm was technically separate from xAI, the arrangement was designed to keep the debt off the company’s books while making the investment attractive to conservative lenders like life insurers. SpaceX’s auditors ultimately determined that the borrowing had to be recorded as company debt, but the Times reports that Musk has already arranged another $40 billion in financing through a separate entity designed to keep that borrowing off SpaceX’s books for now. Similar tactics are reportedly common throughout the industry.

AI hasn’t figured out a way to get the cash under your mattress, though. Just something to consider.
